newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - PolyMASC set for key alliances.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - PolyMASC set for key alliances.

text.p: PolyMASC Pharmaceuticals Plc, the tiny AIM-listed British drug technology group, said on Wednesday it hoped to announce a string of key alliances in the next few months.

In an interview with Reuters, business development and licensing director Stephen Charles said the company was in "active negotiations" to use its drug-enhancement skills in creating a blood cell growth factor treatment for use in diseases like cancer, AIDS and anaemia.

He also hopes to bring talks on a novel anti-cancer drug to a conclusion "in the near future," and unveil a strategic alliance involving liposomes, artificially-made sacs which transport drugs directly to diseased cells.

Behind the optimism is a technology developed at the Royal Free Hospital in Hampstead, north London, which PolyMASC believes can improve a range of new and existing drugs, particularly biotechnology drugs.

The 18-strong company specialises in attaching polyethylene glycol (PEG) to molecules to disguise them and trick the body's natural defences, allowing drugs to get through to their targets more effectively.

The technique, known as PEGylation, can extend the life of molecule-based drugs in the body by up to 400 times, leading to fewer injections and reducing the filtering effect of organs like the liver and kidneys.

Although the technique is more than 20 years old, problems with different methods have restricted its use. But PolyMASC said it had refined the technique with "innocuous chemistry," producing advantages including greater effectiveness, so lower doses were needed, and reduced toxicity.

Charles said rapid growth in biotechnology drugs which use molecules like proteins and peptides to function offers PolyMASC an important platform for growth, especially as they lose patent protection.

"People we are looking at want to get into generic biotech drugs, but it is an enormous investment," said Charles. He said PolyMASC could help create generic drugs which were an improvement on the originals.

As an example he cited the two most successful biotech drugs to date, Amgen Inc's blood cell-boosting drugs Epogen and Neupogen, which had combined sales of more than half a billion dollars in the first three months of 1997.

"Epogen has to be given three times a week, but maybe it could be given once a week," Charles said. He also believes PolyMASC could help many biotech drugs, most of which are injected, to be converted to tablets.

PolyMASC was floated on the Alternative Investment Market (AIM) in London in December 1995, raising 5 million stg. Since then it has struggled to gain analysts' attention among a plethora of competing biotechnology flotations, with the shares underperforming the FTSE pharmaceutical index by 33 percent, according to Reuters 3000 data.

Among analysts who follow PolyMASC, Henry Cooke Lumsden's Tom Geimer has a speculative stance on the stock, while Erling Refsum of Yamaichi rates it a buy as a "relatively low risk enabling technology."
PolyMASC can already point to a number of major partners, including Genzyme Corp of the U.S. and Canada's Cangene Corp, and it is working with U.S.-based Hydro Med Sciences on a cancer vaccine.

As well as licensing technology, which Charles said should break even as an operation by the end of 1998, PolyMASC also has ambitions to develop drugs through clinical trials itself. The two current lead candidates are cancer vaccinations and a blood growth treatment.

"PolyMASC as a business in terms of PEGylating other people's products should be self-sustaining from now on," said Charles, "but in terms of major products we'd need to raise money to maximise returns to our shareholders."
